chain.title: How drought travels
chain.lead: From rain to soil to crops: each step with its delay in months and the strength of the link, measured on monthly anomalies.
chain.conclusion: In Ukraine drought reaches the fields in {ua}; in Australia in {au}.
chain.ghg_note: Greenhouse gases and water vapour drive the slow warming shown on the Trends page. Their effect builds over decades, so it has no monthly delay in this chain.
chain.legend: Thicker arrows mean stronger links. Faded arrows did not pass the test after correcting for many comparisons. A link shows that two things move together, not proof that one causes the other.
expected.title: What weather alone would predict
expected.lead: A model trained only on weather estimates how green the fields should be. The gap between that and the satellite reading shows what weather cannot explain: lost irrigation water, damaged or abandoned fields.
expected.sentence: In {month} {year}, fields in {zone} were {pct}% {dir} green than this weather would predict.
expected.control_note: This is a rainfed control zone. The gap stays close to zero here, which shows the model is not inventing effects.
compare.title: Ukraine and Australia side by side
compare.conclusion: Irrigated vs rainfed fields, compared with their usual gap: {au} in Australia's 2018–19 drought, {ua} in Ukraine after the Kakhovka reservoir was lost.
compare.effect: Irrigated vs rainfed fields during the crisis
compare.lessons: Australia shows that managed water keeps fields going even in a drought: in 2018–19, irrigated fields in the Murrumbidgee were 7% better off against rainfed ones than usual, and irrigation softened drought in all three of our zone pairs. Ukraine after Kakhovka shows the opposite: without the reservoir, irrigated fields fell a further 5% behind rainfed ones (13% in the worst month) and have not recovered. The lesson for southern Ukraine is to rebuild not only the canals but also the rules: water allocations, water trading and a plan for dry years, as in the Murray–Darling Basin. And to act fast, because in Ukraine a rain shortfall reaches the fields in the same month, in Australia within one month. Australia can take a lesson in vulnerability from Ukraine: when a whole region depends on one water source, losing it hits everyone at once, so backup sources and protecting infrastructure are part of drought resilience too.

expert.title: Expert view
expert.lead: Every number behind the app, for researchers and judges.
expert.trends_help: Growing-season averages, Sen's slope per decade, modified Mann-Kendall test, p-values corrected for testing many variables at once (Benjamini–Hochberg).
expert.tool_help: The NASA challenge in five steps: choose a variable, a zone and years, then read the series, its trend and whether it is significant.
expert.tool_result: Trend for the full record: {slope} per decade, {badge}.
expert.tool_note: The tested trend is computed by the pipeline on growing-season averages for the full record; the chart shows the period you picked.
expert.skill_help: Tested on years the model never saw. Lower error than the baselines means the model adds real skill.
expert.limits: A link between two series shows they move together, not that one causes the other.
There is no cropland mask yet: zone averages include roads, villages and pasture.
Soil moisture cells are about 28 km, coarse for small zones; field greenness cells are about 5.5 km.
Monthly field greenness and soil moisture currently end in December 2025, so forecasts for January–June 2026 should be checked against new data when it arrives.
Rainfall for the newest days comes from IMERG Late, an early estimate that is later replaced by the Final version.

Five zones and 23 years are a small sample: the 6-month forecast does not beat a simple baseline and is hidden; the 8-day heat, frost and low-rain forecasts did not prove reliable, only the dry-spell one is shown.
War damage and abandoned fields reduce greenness for reasons weather cannot explain; control zones help separate this, but the war effect could not be separated from model error.

now.data_note: Field greenness and soil moisture are NASA monthly products that currently end in December 2025, so the outlook starts from that month. Rainfall and temperature are newer (see Data updated).
ask.provider_note.pollinations: Your browser sends the question and this zone's computed numbers to Pollinations, a free AI service that needs no account. It answers one question at a time; a reply takes 10–40 seconds.
ask.provider_note.puter: Puter.js opens a sign-in window the first time (a free Puter account), then uses stronger models. Usage counts against your Puter account, not ours.
ask.via: Answered by {model}, using only this app's numbers. Check important decisions with the Expert page.
ask.fallback: The online AI did not answer ({error}), so this answer is built from a template with the same numbers.
map.title: Field condition map
map.lead: Every square is one 5.5 km NASA MODIS cell. Choose a crop's key months, move through the years, then click a field to see its history and plan a crop there.
map.note_year: Green: greener than this field's own 2003–2021 normal in {window}. Brown: drier and paler.
map.note_now: Latest NASA month, compared with the same calendar month in 2003–2021, all vegetation.
map.note_fc: Forecasts are made per zone, not per field: the boxes show the drought light for that zone.
map.note_change: {event}. Each field compared with the whole region, so shared weather cancels out: red = fell behind its neighbours, green = gained.
map.note_best: 0–100: 60% how green this field usually is in these months, 40% how steady it is from year to year (2003–2021). It does not know which crop was grown.
map.pick_hint: Click any field on the map to see its 23-year history and a planting check.
map.outside: This point is outside the area with field data.
map.no_data: No reliable satellite data for this cell (water, town or cloud).
map.cell.history: Condition in these months, year by year
map.cell.poor: Clearly worse than normal in {n} of {total} years: {years}.
map.source: NASA MODIS MOD13C2 v061 NDVI, monthly, 0.05°, to {month}; cloudy and water cells removed.
map.caveats: There is no crop-type map yet, so a cell shows all vegetation, not one crop.
Forecasts and alerts are per zone.
plan.title: Plan a crop
plan.lead: Tell us what you want to grow, where and when. We check 23 years of NASA data for that place: how often the soil was dry at sowing, rain failed, the crop's key months were dry or hot, and frost came late.
plan.pick_on_map: or pick a field on the map
plan.warn.crop_other_country: This crop's calendar is for the other country; results may not fit.
plan.warn.needs_irrigation: This crop is grown only with irrigation here.
plan.warn.no_irrigation_system: This zone has no irrigation system in our data; irrigation is counted only if you have your own water.
plan.warn.kakhovka_water_lost: The Kakhovka irrigation system lost its water source in June 2023. Count on irrigation only if you have another source.
plan.score_meaning.yellow: some risk; plan for dry spells
plan.risk.rain_fail: Rain clearly short in the first two months
plan.risk.dry_key: Soil clearly dry in the key months ({months})
plan.risk.heat: Days above 35 °C in the key months ({months})
plan.risk_help: Share of past years (2003–2025; heat and frost 2015–2025) when this happened in this zone. 'Clearly' means more than one standard deviation from normal. The score adds these risks up; irrigation halves the water risks.
plan.history: How green the key months ({months}) were, each year
plan.history_sum: Clearly poor in {poor} of {total} years, clearly good in {good}.
plan.now_line: Latest NASA month {date}: fields {pct}% vs normal; soil moisture z {soil}.
plan.ranking_help: Best score and month for each zone in this country, with the same irrigation choice.
plan.disclaimer: Crop calendars are typical regional windows, not advice for a specific field. Scores show how risky each choice was in past years from NASA satellite and model data; check them with a local agronomist and seed supplier.
